assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, via Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstrations of record accuracy and stability, are a textbook case of a new measurement technique that moves the precision frontier by orders of magnitude. The fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 are clear and quantifiable, and the clocks have opened relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches and redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the original magic-wavelength proposal (2001-2003) and early Sr lattice clock work. Ye's JILA group built the clocks that reached the accuracy and stability frontier. Two laureates is a clean and fair configuration, though contributions from other Sr and Yb lattice-clock groups (e.g. in Paris, PTB, NIST) exist.
assessment.maturity: Over twenty years of independent confirmation across many laboratories, with stable interpretation. Recognition is timely, as the redefinition of the SI second is being discussed and the technology is mature. Frequency-comb and cold-atom work was already recognized in 2005 and 1997/2001/2012.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier clock and frequency-comb prizes (2005, 2012) may be raised in discussion.
Whether other lattice-clock pioneers should share credit is not settled by the supplied text.
Not fully certain of the precise priority details in the early Sr-clock literature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single NV-center spins in diamond, and their use as nanoscale magnetic, electric and thermal sensors, is a compelling quantum-sensing advance. Room-temperature coherence times, single-spin readout, and applications from nanoscale NMR to biology and condensed matter make it the type of measurement-enabling method I value.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated optical detection of single NV spins (1997) and coherent control. Lukin's group developed quantum-register and nanoscale sensing demonstrations. Awarding these three is plausible, though Awschalom, Hanson, Hollenberg, Walsworth, Yacoby and others made major contributions, so the allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups and commercial devices confirm the results over about 25 years. The field is mature enough in basics, while some sensing applications are still developing.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over a larger community than three names.
Some claimed applications (biology, in-cell sensing) are still maturing.
Possible concern that the prize composition would blur experimental origins with later sensing proposals.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light for quantum-enhanced interferometry has gone from theory to routine operation in gravitational-wave detectors, where it reduces quantum noise in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600. It is a direct case of a quantum-optics technique extending measurement sensitivity beyond the standard quantum limit, with a clear and lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed squeezed-vacuum injection into interferometers (1981). Experimental squeezing was first shown by Slusher et al. and Kimble's group (1985-86); Schnabel and the GEO600 team (with Mavalvala, McKenna, Vahlbruch and others) did key demonstration and implementation work. The list excludes some experimental pioneers, and the three-name choice is a compromise with an unresolved credit question.
assessment.maturity: Observatory-scale implementation is established and independently confirmed by multiple detectors. Recognition is timely given the 2017 Nobel for gravitational-wave detection, though that may argue that the field has been recognized already.
uncertainties: Substantial credit ambiguity among theorists, early experimenters, and implementers (e.g. Slusher, Walls, Mavalvala).
Overlap with the LIGO prize (2017) may reduce committee appetite.
I am not able to verify each priority claim independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry provides precision measurement of gravity, rotation and fundamental constants, with matter-wave interferometers reaching remarkable sensitivity. It is a clear new measurement principle with many applications, from tests of the equivalence principle to geodesy and navigation.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard and Mlynek demonstrated early atom interferometers (1991, with Chu/Bordé and Kasevich also in 1991). Kasevich and Chu showed the laser-based gravimeter and gradiometer. Steven Chu and Christian Bordé are not in the credited names, which leaves an unresolved attribution question; three names are a reasonable subset only partly.
assessment.maturity: Mature for lab precision measurements, with independent confirmations. Field applications and large-scale gravitational-wave or dark-matter experiments are still developing, so the final impact is partially premature.
uncertainties: Missing key names (Chu, Bordé) weaken any fair allocation among the supplied names.
Overlap with the 1997 and 2001 laser-cooling and BEC prizes.
Practical device impact is still growing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson at the LHC in 2012 was a defining measurement in particle physics, confirming a central prediction. The detectors, analysis and independent confirmation are of the very highest scientific importance.
assessment.attribution: ATLAS and CMS are collaborations of thousands, and the 2013 prize went to the theorists. The supplied names are spokespersons and detector proposers: Gianotti (ATLAS spokesperson at announcement), Della Negra and Virdee (CMS leaders and founders), Jenni (ATLAS founder). Any three-person subset is difficult to defend and the collaboration rule limits a fair allocation.
assessment.maturity: Entirely mature and independently confirmed by two experiments, with properties continuing to be measured. Recognition is not premature, but it is delayed relative to the theory prize.
uncertainties: Allocation of credit among thousands of collaborators is unresolved and may be committee-blocking.
The choice of three of four credited names is arbitrary.
The 2013 prize already recognized the mechanism.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation of Hubbard models with ultracold atoms, including the Mott insulator transition and Fermi-Hubbard physics, opened a controlled-experiment route to many-body physics, with quantum gas microscopes giving single-site readout. The impact on the field of quantum simulation is large and the experimental demonstration is clear.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard simulator; Greiner and Bloch observed the superfluid-Mott transition (2002); Esslinger demonstrated fermionic Mott insulators. Greiner is also decisive for quantum gas microscopes. Choosing three of four credited names is a judgment call and Hänsch and Zoller overlap with other candidates.
assessment.maturity: Substantial independent confirmation. The field of cold-atom simulation is mature in demonstration but still working toward results that exceed classical computation, so the scientific payoff continues.
uncertainties: Fair allocation among four credited names is unresolved.
Overlap with other atomic quantum-information candidates (Zoller, Bloch).
Some physics claims (e.g. high-Tc relevance) remain open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Aberration-corrected electron optics broke through the limits of electron lenses and made routine sub-angstrom imaging in transmission microscopy possible. It is a pure instrument and method advance that has changed materials physics, a type of progress that I value because it enabled widespread observation of atomic structure.
assessment.attribution: The trio of Rose (theory of correction), Haider (implementation for TEM, with Rose, Uhlemann and others) and Urban (STEM/TEM correctors for materials) is the commonly proposed combination, with Krivanek an obvious potential contender who is not credited here. This leaves some doubt about completeness of the proposed configuration.
assessment.maturity: Very mature; correctors are commercial and widespread, and independent confirmation is overwhelming. Recognition is somewhat late but timely given the 1986 Ruska prize precedent for electron optics.
uncertainties: Krivanek's omission is a possible attribution issue.
Whether this fits as physics rather than materials science or chemistry may divide the committee.
Priority details between corrector designs are not independently checked.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Light-matter quantum interfaces provide the foundational ideas and demonstrations for quantum networks, such as quantum repeaters and memories with atomic ensembles and single atoms. This is close to my own field of quantum memories in solids; I know how hard real efficiency and coherence are, and I value the concept's impact on quantum communication.
assessment.attribution: The proposals of Cirac and Zoller on quantum state transfer and Kimble's cavity-QED and atomic-ensemble demonstrations are central. Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller repeater ideas and experimental work by Lukin, Polzik, Gisin, Kuzmich and rare-earth groups are important and not credited here, so the three names do not cover all decisive contributions.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are advancing steadily but practical quantum networks and repeaters remain largely in development. Recognition could be considered premature relative to the performance requirements for real devices.
uncertainties: Compound subject spanning theory proposals and diverse experimental platforms.
Practical efficiency and scalability are not yet demonstrated.
Credit among numerous groups is broad.
